title: What's the Matter with Indiana? 2026
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: The Science of Reading Classroom newsletter investigates a stark discrepancy in Indiana's own data: the state's Secretary of Education publicly celebrated 90 percent third-grade reading proficiency, but only 42 percent of the same cohort passed the state's own ILEARN ELA assessment that year. After working through released items from both tests herself, the author concludes the gap has nothing to do with instruction and everything to do with test design: the IREAD is an easy, narrowly phonics-focused screener while the ILEARN demands close reading of culturally dense, background-knowledge-dependent passages. She recommends Indiana retire the IREAD as a proficiency claim (it can only flag functional illiteracy, not diagnose reading skill), stop over-interpreting the ILEARN as a pure comprehension measure when it is really testing background knowledge, and cut back on the 8-12 hours of testing third graders undergo annually. A closing anecdote about a student who scored perfectly on the IREAD while testing below benchmark on DIBELS oral reading fluency makes the stakes concrete: a test that flatters state officials can simultaneously fail an individual child who actually needs support.
points: The core diagnostic finding is procedural, not political: nearly 90% pass the IREAD because it is an easy test (word-ending-sound recognition, no reading of instructions required) while only 42% pass the ILEARN because it demands close reading of dense, knowledge-loaded passages — the same cohort, two very different instruments.

The author's recommendation to retire the IREAD is specific and falsifiable: it can identify functionally illiterate students but 'doesn't screen for or identify particular reading deficits,' making it unfit to certify grade-level reading proficiency the way the state secretary's op-ed implied.

Citing Natalie Wexler's prior argument, the piece reframes the ILEARN itself as 'more a test of student background knowledge' than pure reading comprehension, arguing state reading tests should be built around content drawn from science and social studies standards to level the playing field.

The closing case study, a student with a perfect IREAD score but a below-benchmark DIBELS composite (weak oral reading fluency and nonsense word fluency), makes the stakes concrete: an easy proficiency test can mask real reading deficits state officials have already certified as fine.
quotes: Last month, Indiana's Secretary of Education, Katie Jenner, wrote an op-ed, declaring that in 2026, nearly 90 percent of Indiana third grade students were reading proficiently. Sounds like cause for celebration, right? Not so fast. In the same year, only 42% of the same group of students passed the statewide ILEARN ELA assessment.
The answer is actually quite simple. Nearly 90% of Indiana 3rd graders pass the IREAD because it is a very easy test. Approximately 40% pass the ILEARN ELA because it is a hard test. Case closed.

The IREAD can identify the small percentage of Indiana 3rd graders who are functionally illiterate. That's all it can do. It's not diagnostic. It doesn't screen for or identify particular reading deficits.
The ILEARN, like other state reading tests, purports to measure student reading comprehension. In reality, it's more a test of student background knowledge.

My colleague administered the DIBELS to learn more, finding that her composite score was below benchmark, with particular weaknesses in oral reading fluency and nonsense word fluency. The IREAD failed to detect any of these challenges.
Her state's Secretary of Education will count her as a proficient reader, but she is not.
